candidate.answerReason: Central entries 4, 5, and 6 contribute 12, 18, and 12 arrays, respectively, giving 42.

methods.label: Count by the central entry
methods.explanation:
The central entry has three entries that must be smaller: those directly above it, directly to its left, and diagonally above and left. Similarly, three entries must be larger. Thus the central entry can only be \(4\), \(5\), or \(6\). Also, \(1\) must occupy the upper left corner and \(9\) the lower right corner.

Suppose the central entry is \(4\). The three smaller entries must be \(1,2,3\), with \(2\) and \(3\) interchangeable between the top middle and middle left cells. This gives \(2\) choices. Among the remaining cells, \(9\) is fixed, and \(5,6,7,8\) form two increasing pairs: the top right and middle right cells, and the bottom left and bottom middle cells. Choose which two digits belong to the right pair; their order, and the order of the other pair, are then forced. There are \(3+2+1=6\) choices of a two-digit subset, so this case gives \(2\cdot6=12\) arrays.

Rotating an array by \(180^\circ\) and replacing each digit \(d\) by \(10-d\) preserves increasing rows and columns and exchanges central entries \(4\) and \(6\). Applying this transformation twice restores the original array, so it pairs the two cases exactly. The central-entry-\(6\) case therefore also gives \(12\) arrays.

Now suppose the central entry is \(5\). Three of the four smaller digits occupy the cells above and left of the center. The remaining smaller digit must occupy either the top right or bottom left cell, since every other cell is forced to exceed \(5\).

First take the top right cell to be smaller than \(5\). The digits \(1,2,3,4\) fill the top row and the middle left cell. After placing \(1\), choose the middle left entry from \(2,3,4\); the remaining two digits fill the top row in increasing order. This gives \(3\) choices. For the larger digits, \(9\) is fixed at the bottom right. Choose the middle right entry from \(6,7,8\), and place the other two digits in increasing order along the bottom row. This gives another \(3\) choices. Comparisons between these smaller and larger groups are automatic, so there are \(3\cdot3=9\) arrays. Transposing the array gives exactly \(9\) arrays in which the bottom left cell is smaller than \(5\). These two cases are disjoint, giving \(18\) arrays with central entry \(5\).

Every valid array has exactly one of the three central entries considered, and each set of choices determines one array. Hence the total is
\[
12+18+12=\boxed{42},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{D}\).

Center 5 has two disjoint transpose-related cases, each with 3·3=9 arrays. All row and column comparisons are satisfied, and the exhaustive total is 42.
